task_4.title: Add new gallery showcasing flexible indexes capabilities
task_4.description: A new gallery was added to the xarray-indexes documentation site (xarray-indexes.readthedocs.io) to demonstrate the possibilities enabled by flexible indexes. This is a documentation-only change with no associated code modifications in the library itself.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the xarray-indexes documentation includes a gallery section that showcases the capabilities and use-case patterns enabled by the flexible indexes feature, providing users with practical examples and demonstrations.

expectation.grounded: The xarray-indexes ReadTheDocs site at xarray-indexes.readthedocs.io should host a new gallery section. No runtime APIs, return types, or library behavior are affected. The gallery should be accessible and render correctly on the documentation site.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to browse a dedicated gallery on the xarray-indexes documentation site that illustrates what flexible indexes enable, helping them understand available patterns and use cases without needing to discover them from source code or API references alone.

constraints.grounded: No changes to the xarray public API, runtime behavior, or any Python module. The gallery is purely a documentation artifact hosted on ReadTheDocs. Existing documentation pages and cross-references must remain intact and unbroken.
constraints.conceptual: This change must not alter any library functionality or runtime behavior. Existing documentation must not be disrupted. The gallery must be purely additive documentation content.

behavior: A new gallery page or section is available on the xarray-indexes ReadTheDocs documentation site.
The gallery demonstrates possibilities enabled by flexible indexes.
No runtime, API, or behavioral changes occur in the xarray library itself.
acceptance_criteria: When a user navigates to the xarray-indexes ReadTheDocs site, they should find a gallery section showcasing flexible index capabilities.
When the documentation is built, the gallery renders correctly with no broken links or missing content.
When upgrading from 2025.7.0 to 2025.7.1, no existing API behavior, imports, or runtime functionality should change as a result of this addition.

task_3.title: Raise error when custom index creates extra variables in set_xindex
task_3.description: Dataset.set_xindex() previously silently ignored any extra variables returned by a custom index's create_variables() method that did not match the provided coordinate names. This was confusing for users building advanced custom indexes (e.g., weather forecast indexes that compute derived coordinates). The fix replaces the silent-ignore behavior with a clear ValueError that identifies the extra variables and suggests using the factory method pattern via Coordinates.from_xindex() and Dataset.assign_coords() as an alternative workflow.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Dataset.set_xindex() no longer silently ignores extra variables returned by a custom index's create_variables() method. When a custom index creates variables whose names are not in the list of coordinate names passed to set_xindex(), a clear error must be raised instead of discarding those variables without warning. The error message must guide users toward the recommended factory method pattern using Coordinates.from_xindex() and Dataset.assign_coords().

expectation.grounded: When Dataset.set_xindex() is called and the custom index's create_variables() returns variable names that are not a subset of the coordinate names, a ValueError must be raised. The error must list the extra variable names and the expected coordinate names, and must reference the factory method pattern involving Coordinates.from_xindex() and Dataset.assign_coords(). When create_variables() returns only variables matching the coordinate names, set_xindex() must continue to work as before with no error.
expectation.conceptual: When a custom index produces additional variables beyond those corresponding to the requested coordinates, set_xindex() must reject the operation with an informative error rather than silently dropping the extra variables. The error must clearly identify which variables are unexpected and suggest the recommended alternative approach for advanced use cases.

constraints.grounded: Existing custom indexes whose create_variables() returns only variables matching the coordinate names must continue to work without any change in behavior. The error must only trigger when the set of returned variable names is a strict superset of the coordinate names. The ValueError must include both the extra variable names and the coordinate names for diagnostic clarity. No extra variables may be silently discarded.
constraints.conceptual: Backward compatibility must be preserved for all custom indexes that do not produce extra variables. The change must only affect the case where extraneous variables are returned. The error must be actionable, providing enough context for the user to understand what went wrong and how to achieve their goal through an alternative API path.

behavior: Dataset.set_xindex() compares the variable names returned by the custom index's create_variables() against the coordinate names provided to set_xindex().

If extra variable names are detected (names present in create_variables() output but not in the coordinate names list), a ValueError is raised immediately before any variables or indexes are applied to the dataset.
The ValueError message enumerates the extra variable names and the expected coordinate names.
The ValueError message suggests the factory method pattern: constructing the index, calling Coordinates.from_xindex(), and using Dataset.assign_coords().
When PandasMultiIndex is involved, the dimension name is prepended to the coordinate names list before the extra-variable check is performed.
If create_variables() returns only variables matching the coordinate names, behavior is unchanged from the previous version.
acceptance_criteria: When a custom index's create_variables() returns a variable name not in the coordinate names passed to set_xindex(), calling set_xindex() raises a ValueError.
The ValueError message includes the names of the extra variables and the names of the expected coordinates.
The ValueError message references Coordinates.from_xindex() and Dataset.assign_coords() as the recommended alternative.
When a custom index's create_variables() returns only variables matching the coordinate names, set_xindex() completes successfully with no error.
When set_xindex() is used with a PandasMultiIndex, the index dimension is included in the coordinate names used for the extra-variable check, preserving correct behavior for multi-indexes.
No extra variables are silently discarded under any circumstances — they either cause an error or are part of the expected coordinate set.

task_2.title: Add create_default_indexes parameter to skip index creation when opening datasets
task_2.description: Introduces a new boolean parameter `create_default_indexes` (default True) to `open_dataset`, `open_dataarray`, `open_datatree`, `open_groups`, and `open_zarr` that allows users to skip the automatic creation of default pandas indexes for dimension coordinates when opening datasets. When set to False, coordinate data is not eagerly loaded into memory, enabling significant memory savings for large datasets. The backend entrypoint (`StoreBackendEntrypoint`) is refactored so that it no longer creates indexes by default, deferring index creation to the top-level API layer based on this parameter.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: When opening large datasets, xarray eagerly creates pandas indexes for all dimension coordinates, which forces the coordinate data to be loaded into memory even when the user does not need indexed access. Ensure that users can opt out of automatic default index creation when opening datasets via `open_dataset`, `open_dataarray`, `open_datatree`, `open_groups`, and `open_zarr` by passing `create_default_indexes=False`, thereby avoiding unnecessary memory consumption.

expectation.grounded: A new boolean parameter `create_default_indexes` (default `True`) is added to `xr.open_dataset`, `xr.open_dataarray`, `xr.open_datatree`, `xr.open_groups`, and `xr.open_zarr`. When `create_default_indexes=True`, dimension coordinates that have a single matching dimension and are not already indexed receive a default pandas index via `Coordinates` assignment (through the internal `_maybe_create_default_indexes` helper). When `create_default_indexes=False`, the dataset is returned without default indexes and coordinate data remains lazy (not loaded into memory). The `StoreBackendEntrypoint.open_dataset` constructs datasets with an explicit `Coordinates` object passing `indexes={}`, so backends no longer create default indexes themselves; index creation is the responsibility of the top-level API functions. For `DataTree` paths, `_maybe_create_default_indexes` is applied via `map_over_datasets`. Chunking logic (via `_chunk_ds`) operates on the already-index-resolved dataset rather than the raw backend dataset.
expectation.conceptual: Users can pass `create_default_indexes=False` to any of the dataset-opening functions to prevent automatic creation of pandas indexes for dimension coordinates. By default (True), behavior is unchanged from prior versions. When disabled, coordinate variables remain present in the dataset but are not indexed, and their underlying data is not eagerly loaded into memory. This applies uniformly to single datasets, data arrays, data trees, and grouped opens.

constraints.grounded: When `create_default_indexes=True` (the default), the observable behavior of `open_dataset`, `open_dataarray`, `open_datatree`, `open_groups`, and `open_zarr` must be identical to the previous version — all dimension coordinates must receive default pandas indexes. The `Coordinates` object created in `StoreBackendEntrypoint` must pass `indexes={}` so that the backend itself does not create any indexes. Backends may still create their own custom indexes regardless of this parameter. Chunking via dask or other chunked array types must work correctly with both `create_default_indexes=True` and `create_default_indexes=False` — the chunk operation must receive the index-resolved (or index-skipped) dataset, not the raw backend dataset.
constraints.conceptual: Default behavior must remain backward-compatible: existing code that does not pass the new parameter must produce identical results with indexes created as before. Skipping default indexes must not break chunked (lazy) loading. Backends retain the ability to create their own custom indexes independent of this parameter. The parameter must be consistently available across all top-level dataset-opening functions.

behavior: When `create_default_indexes=False` is passed to `open_dataset`, the returned Dataset contains dimension coordinates without pandas indexes and without eagerly loading coordinate data into memory.

When `create_default_indexes=True` (default), dimension coordinates that share their name with their sole dimension and are not already indexed receive a default pandas index, preserving backward-compatible behavior.

The `StoreBackendEntrypoint` no longer creates indexes during backend dataset construction; it splits variables into data vars and coordinate vars and constructs a `Coordinates` object with an empty indexes dict.
For `open_datatree`, `_maybe_create_default_indexes` is applied across all nodes in the tree via `map_over_datasets` when `create_default_indexes=True`.
Chunking is now performed on the index-resolved dataset rather than directly on the raw backend dataset, ensuring consistency between indexed and non-indexed paths.
The `open_zarr` convenience function accepts and forwards `create_default_indexes` to `open_dataset`.
Close handlers from backend dataset nodes are properly propagated to the final dataset/tree when either `create_default_indexes` or `chunks` processing has occurred.
acceptance_criteria: When calling `xr.open_dataset(path, create_default_indexes=False)`, the returned Dataset should have dimension coordinates present but with no associated pandas indexes, and coordinate data should not be loaded into memory.

When calling `xr.open_dataset(path)` or `xr.open_dataset(path, create_default_indexes=True)`, the returned Dataset should have pandas indexes for all dimension coordinates, identical to behavior before this change.
When calling `xr.open_dataarray(path, create_default_indexes=False)`, the returned DataArray's parent Dataset should have no default indexes on its dimension coordinates.
When calling `xr.open_datatree(path, create_default_indexes=False)`, no node in the returned DataTree should have default pandas indexes for its dimension coordinates.
When calling `xr.open_groups(path, create_default_indexes=False)`, each returned Dataset in the groups dict should have no default pandas indexes.
When calling `xr.open_zarr(path, create_default_indexes=False)`, the returned Dataset should have no default pandas indexes for dimension coordinates.
When combining `create_default_indexes=False` with `chunks` (e.g., `chunks='auto'`), the dataset should be correctly chunked and coordinate data should remain lazy.
When combining `create_default_indexes=True` with `chunks`, the dataset should have both indexes and chunked data variables, matching prior behavior.
Coordinates that already have an index assigned by the backend should not receive a duplicate default index when `create_default_indexes=True`.

task_1.title: Add NDPointIndex for nearest-neighbor selection on irregular n-dimensional data
task_1.description: Introduces a new xarray.indexes.NDPointIndex that enables label-based nearest-neighbor selection on datasets with irregular, n-dimensional coordinates. The index uses scipy.spatial.KDTree by default and is created via Dataset.set_xindex or DataArray.set_xindex from existing coordinate variables. It supports point-wise selection through .sel() with method='nearest', accepting scalar, Variable, DataArray, and array-like labels with automatic broadcasting. A pluggable TreeAdapter abstraction allows alternative spatial tree backends. The index also provides rudimentary equality-based alignment support.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that xarray provides a built-in index for performing nearest-neighbor label-based selection on irregular, n-dimensional data (e.g., unstructured grids with multi-dimensional coordinates). Previously, users had to rely on external packages like xoak for this capability. The new index should integrate with xarray's existing .sel() API and support common label types including scalars, Variables, DataArrays, and plain array-likes with broadcasting semantics.

expectation.grounded: NDPointIndex is publicly available at xarray.indexes.NDPointIndex and TreeAdapter at xarray.indexes.TreeAdapter. NDPointIndex.from_variables() constructs the index from coordinate variables, validating that all variables share the same dimensions and shape and that the number of variables equals the number of dimensions, raising ValueError on mismatch. The default tree backend is ScipyKDTreeAdapter (wrapping scipy.spatial.KDTree), but a custom TreeAdapter subclass can be supplied via the 'tree_adapter_cls' option. NDPointIndex.sel() only supports method='nearest' and raises ValueError for any other method value. It requires labels for all associated coordinate names, raising ValueError if any are missing. Accepted label types are DataArray, Variable, scalar, or array-like with ndim matching the coordinate variables' ndim; other label types raise ValueError. Labels are broadcast against each other before querying. NDPointIndex.equals() returns False when comparing against a non-NDPointIndex or when the underlying tree adapter types differ, and delegates to TreeAdapter.equals() otherwise. NDPointIndex.rename() returns self when no relevant coordinate or dimension names are affected, or a new instance with updated names otherwise.
expectation.conceptual: A new index type should be available that enables nearest-neighbor point-wise selection on datasets with irregular multi-dimensional coordinates. Users create the index via set_xindex by specifying the coordinate variables that define the spatial location of data points. Selection is performed through the standard .sel() API with method='nearest', supporting scalar values, Variable and DataArray objects, and plain array-like objects as labels, with automatic broadcasting across label inputs. The index should support equality comparison for alignment and renaming of coordinates and dimensions. The spatial tree backend should be pluggable to allow alternative implementations beyond the default KDTree.

constraints.grounded: All coordinate variables associated with the NDPointIndex must share identical dimensions and shape; from_variables() must raise ValueError otherwise. The number of coordinate variables must equal the number of coordinate dimensions; from_variables() must raise ValueError on mismatch. NDPointIndex.sel() must only accept method='nearest' and must raise ValueError for any other method. All coordinate names must be provided as labels during sel(); missing labels must raise ValueError. Array-like labels must have the same number of dimensions as the coordinate variables; otherwise sel() must raise ValueError. TreeAdapter.equals() raises NotImplementedError by default if not overridden by a subclass. The index must not support chunked (dask) coordinates.
constraints.conceptual: The index only supports nearest-neighbor selection, not exact matching or range queries. All associated coordinates must be uniformly shaped and dimensioned. Every coordinate must receive a label during selection. Plain array labels must match the dimensionality of the indexed coordinates. The default tree adapter requires scipy as a dependency. The index does not support chunked or lazily-evaluated coordinates.

behavior: NDPointIndex is now importable from xarray.indexes and listed in xarray.indexes.__all__
TreeAdapter abstract base class is now importable from xarray.indexes and listed in xarray.indexes.__all__
Calling Dataset.set_xindex or DataArray.set_xindex with NDPointIndex builds a spatial tree from the specified coordinate variables
NDPointIndex.from_variables() raises ValueError when coordinate variables have differing dimensions or shapes
NDPointIndex.from_variables() raises ValueError when the number of variables does not match the number of coordinate dimensions
NDPointIndex.from_variables() defaults to ScipyKDTreeAdapter when no 'tree_adapter_cls' option is provided
NDPointIndex.sel() raises ValueError when method is not 'nearest'
NDPointIndex.sel() raises ValueError when labels are not provided for all associated coordinate names
NDPointIndex.sel() accepts DataArray, Variable, scalar, and matching-ndim array-like labels
NDPointIndex.sel() raises ValueError for array-like labels whose ndim does not match the coordinate variables' ndim
Scalar and Variable/DataArray labels are broadcast against each other before querying the tree
Query results are unraveled from flat indices back into per-dimension indexers matching the label shape and dimensions
NDPointIndex.equals() returns False for non-NDPointIndex or differing tree adapter types, and delegates to the adapter's equals() otherwise
NDPointIndex.rename() returns self when no relevant names are affected; otherwise returns a new instance with updated coordinate names and dimensions
NDPointIndex._repr_inline_() displays the class name and the tree adapter type name
acceptance_criteria: When a user imports xarray.indexes.NDPointIndex, the class is available without error
When a user imports xarray.indexes.TreeAdapter, the abstract class is available without error
When a user calls ds.set_xindex(('xx', 'yy'), NDPointIndex) on a dataset with 2D coordinates xx and yy sharing the same dims and shape, the dataset gains an NDPointIndex shown in its repr
When from_variables() is called with coordinate variables having different dimensions, it should raise ValueError indicating variables must have the same dimensions and shape
When from_variables() is called with a number of variables not matching the number of dimensions, it should raise ValueError indicating the mismatch
When .sel() is called without method='nearest', it should raise ValueError indicating only nearest selection is supported
When .sel() is called with missing labels for one or more coordinates, it should raise ValueError listing the missing coordinate names
When .sel() is called with scalar labels for all coordinates and method='nearest', it should return a scalar (0-dimensional) result with the nearest data point
When .sel() is called with Variable labels for all coordinates and method='nearest', it should return results with the Variable's dimensions and nearest-neighbor values
When .sel() is called with DataArray labels for all coordinates and method='nearest', the labels should be broadcast and results should have the broadcasted dimensions
When .sel() is called with plain array-like labels whose ndim matches the coordinate ndim, results should use the coordinate dimension names as implicit label dimensions
When .sel() is called with array-like labels whose ndim does not match the coordinate variables' ndim, it should raise ValueError
When two NDPointIndex instances built from identical coordinate data are compared via equals(), it should return True
When two NDPointIndex instances built from different coordinate data are compared via equals(), it should return False
When rename() is called with names not affecting the index's coordinates or dimensions, the same index object should be returned
When rename() is called with names affecting coordinates or dimensions, a new index with updated names should be returned

task_5.title: Lazy repr for RangeIndex, MultiIndex, and CoordinateTransform coordinate variables
task_5.description: Coordinate variables backed by pandas.RangeIndex, pandas.MultiIndex, or xarray.indexes.CoordinateTransform are now treated as lazy (not in-memory) for representation purposes. Previously, displaying such variables in Xarray data reprs triggered a full conversion of the underlying index into a numpy array, which for large indexes (e.g., a RangeIndex with 2 billion elements) could allocate gigabytes of memory. The indexing adapter classes were refactored so that their _in_memory property correctly reflects laziness, and the repr formatting functions slice the adapter directly via BasicIndexer rather than materializing the entire array first.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that displaying the repr of an Xarray Dataset or DataArray whose coordinates wrap a large pandas.RangeIndex, pandas.MultiIndex, or CoordinateTransform does not trigger full materialization of the index into a numpy array. Previously, calling repr() or _repr_html_() on such objects could allocate memory proportional to the full index size (e.g., 16 GB for a 2-billion-element RangeIndex), causing out-of-memory conditions or severe performance degradation.

expectation.grounded: PandasIndexingAdapter._in_memory must return False when the underlying array is a pd.RangeIndex. PandasMultiIndexingAdapter._in_memory must always return False. CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter._in_memory must always return False. Variable._in_memory must delegate to the adapter's _in_memory property when the variable's data is a PandasIndexingAdapter or CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter, rather than unconditionally treating PandasIndexingAdapter-backed variables as in-memory. The formatting functions first_n_items and last_n_items must wrap their indexers in BasicIndexer when operating on ExplicitlyIndexed arrays, enabling direct slicing of the adapter without full array conversion. PandasIndexingAdapter._repr_inline_ must use format_array_flat to produce an inline repr without loading the full array. CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter._repr_inline_ must similarly use format_array_flat directly on self rather than materializing a subset array first.
expectation.conceptual: Coordinate variables that wrap memory-efficient index structures (range-based indexes, multi-indexes, and coordinate transforms) must be recognized as lazy by the Variable layer. When their textual or HTML representation is requested, only the elements needed for display should be computed or retrieved, not the entire index. The repr output should still show representative values (head and tail elements) but must not allocate memory proportional to the full index size.

constraints.grounded: Existing indexing behavior of PandasIndexingAdapter, PandasMultiIndexingAdapter, and CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter must be preserved: __getitem__, _oindex_get, and _vindex_get must return the same types and values as before. Scalar conversion via _convert_scalar must remain unchanged. The nbytes property must still report accurate byte sizes. The _repr_inline_ output for PandasMultiIndexingAdapter with level=None must still return the string 'MultiIndex'. Variables backed by regular (non-RangeIndex) pandas indexes, plain numpy arrays, or PandasExtensionArray must continue to report _in_memory as True.
constraints.conceptual: The refactoring must not alter the observable indexing semantics or the values produced by coordinate variable access. Non-lazy coordinate variables (e.g., those backed by standard pandas indexes or numpy arrays) must continue to behave as in-memory. The repr content should still display meaningful sample values for lazy coordinates, just without the cost of full materialization.

behavior: Variable._in_memory returns False for variables whose underlying data is a PandasIndexingAdapter wrapping a pd.RangeIndex
Variable._in_memory returns False for variables whose underlying data is a PandasMultiIndexingAdapter (regardless of the MultiIndex contents)
Variable._in_memory returns False for variables whose underlying data is a CoordinateTransformIndexingAdapter
Variable._in_memory continues to return True for variables backed by PandasIndexingAdapter wrapping non-RangeIndex pandas indexes
Calling repr() or _repr_html_() on a Dataset or DataArray with a large RangeIndex coordinate does not allocate memory proportional to the index size
Calling repr() or _repr_html_() on a Dataset or DataArray with a large MultiIndex coordinate does not first convert the full MultiIndex to a numpy array
Calling repr() or _repr_html_() on a Dataset or DataArray with a CoordinateTransform coordinate does not generate the full coordinate array
The inline repr for lazy coordinates still displays representative head and tail values via format_array_flat
first_n_items and last_n_items correctly slice ExplicitlyIndexed arrays by wrapping indexers in BasicIndexer
PandasIndexingAdapter consolidates indexing logic into a single _index_get method that handles key unpacking, multidimensional fallback, and result wrapping
PandasMultiIndexingAdapter delegates all indexing to the parent _index_get and propagates the level attribute on the result
acceptance_criteria: When a PandasIndex wrapping pd.RangeIndex(2_000_000_000) is used as a coordinate, calling repr() on the resulting Dataset should complete quickly without allocating ~16 GB of memory
When a PandasIndex wrapping pd.RangeIndex(N) is used as a coordinate, the Variable._in_memory property should return False
When a PandasIndex wrapping a standard pd.Index (non-RangeIndex) is used as a coordinate, Variable._in_memory should return True
When a PandasMultiIndex is used as a coordinate, Variable._in_memory should return False
When a CoordinateTransform-based index (e.g., RangeIndex.arange) is used as a coordinate, Variable._in_memory should return False
When repr() is called on a DataArray with a large RangeIndex coordinate, the inline repr should display sample values (head and tail) formatted by format_array_flat
When repr() is called on a DataArray with a MultiIndex coordinate at level=None, the inline repr should display the string 'MultiIndex'
When repr() is called on a DataArray with a MultiIndex coordinate at a specific level, the inline repr should display sample level values via format_array_flat
Indexing operations (__getitem__, oindex, vindex) on PandasIndexingAdapter and PandasMultiIndexingAdapter should return the same values and types as before the refactor
The nbytes property of PandasIndexingAdapter should return correct byte counts using the resolved numpy dtype
